subject: science

items.q: In every chemical reaction, what happens to the atoms?
items.correct: They are rearranged into new substances
items.misconception: Some of them are used up and then destroyed
items.why: Follow the atoms. Count them before and after: the same atoms are there, joined in new substances. Things that seem to vanish have usually become gases or dissolved substances.
items.specStatementText: chemical reactions as the rearrangement of atoms
items.random_wrong: Some change into atoms of other elements

items.q: The diagram shows hydrogen reacting with chlorine. Which statement about the reaction is correct?
items.correct: The same atoms are joined in a new way
items.misconception: The atoms have changed into new atoms
items.why: Atoms keep their identity. A copper coating comes from copper atoms that were already in the solution; hydrogen gas comes from the acid; carbon can only come from something that contains carbon.
items.specStatementText: chemical reactions as the rearrangement of atoms
items.random_wrong: Some of the atoms have been used up

items.q: The diagram shows the particles before and after some water is heated. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: No new substance forms: not a reaction
items.misconception: A gas forms, so it is a chemical reaction
items.why: Ask whether the particles have changed. Ice, water and steam are all made of the same water molecules, so a change of state makes no new substance.
items.specStatementText: chemical reactions as the rearrangement of atoms
items.random_wrong: The water has split into hydrogen and oxygen

items.q: Which of these changes is a chemical reaction?
items.correct: Wood burning on a bonfire
items.misconception: Sugar dissolving in hot tea
items.why: A dissolved solid is still there: the solution weighs as much as the water and sugar did, and evaporating the water gets the sugar back. No new substance has formed.
items.specStatementText: chemical reactions as the rearrangement of atoms
items.random_wrong: Chocolate melting in the sun

items.q: Iron reacts with sulfur to make a single product. Which word equation is correct?
items.correct: iron + sulfur → iron sulfide
items.misconception: iron + sulfur → iron sulfate
items.why: Check what reacted. If there was no oxygen in the reactants, the product cannot be an -ate.
items.specStatementText: representing chemical reactions using formulae and using equations
items.random_wrong: iron sulfide → iron + sulfur

items.q: Magnesium (Mg) burns in oxygen (O₂) to make magnesium oxide (MgO). Which symbol equation is balanced and correct?
items.correct: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO
items.misconception: 2Mg + O₂ → Mg₂O₂
items.why: Formulae are fixed. Put a big number in front of a whole formula and recount every atom.
items.specStatementText: representing chemical reactions using formulae and using equations
items.random_wrong: Mg + O₂ → 2MgO

items.q: The diagram shows hydrogen reacting with oxygen to make water. Which symbol equation matches the diagram?
items.correct: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
items.misconception: H₂ + O₂ → H₂O₂
items.why: Write the correct formula of each product first (water is H₂O). Then balance with big numbers in front, never by joining or changing formulae.
items.specStatementText: representing chemical reactions using formulae and using equations
items.random_wrong: H₂ + O₂ → H₂O

items.q: How many oxygen atoms are on each side of this equation? CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
items.correct: Left 4, right 4
items.misconception: Left 2, right 3
items.why:
Count the atoms in one formula, then multiply by the big number in front. 2O₂ is two O₂ molecules: 2 × 2 = 4 oxygen atoms.

Working: Left: 2O₂ = 2 × 2 = 4 oxygen atoms. Right: CO₂ has 2 oxygen atoms, and 2H₂O = 2 × 1 = 2 oxygen atoms, so 2 + 2 = 4. Left 4, right 4: oxygen is balanced.
items.specStatementText: representing chemical reactions using formulae and using equations
items.random_wrong: Left 4, right 3
items.working: Left: 2O₂ = 2 × 2 = 4 oxygen atoms. Right: CO₂ has 2 oxygen atoms, and 2H₂O = 2 × 1 = 2 oxygen atoms, so 2 + 2 = 4. Left 4, right 4: oxygen is balanced.

items.q: The diagram shows methane burning in plenty of oxygen. Where do the hydrogen atoms from the methane end up?
items.correct: In the water molecules made
items.misconception: In hydrogen gas molecules
items.why: Oxygen joins with both: the carbon atoms end up in carbon dioxide and the hydrogen atoms end up in water.
items.specStatementText: combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions
items.random_wrong: Turned into heat and light

items.q: Magnesium burns in air with a bright white flame. Which substance is made?
items.correct: Solid magnesium oxide
items.misconception: Soot made of carbon
items.why: Ask which atoms were there. A metal and oxygen can only make a metal oxide; soot needs carbon atoms, which come only from something that contains carbon.
items.specStatementText: combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions
items.random_wrong: Carbon dioxide and water

items.q: Calcium carbonate is heated strongly. What does it form?
items.correct: Calcium oxide and carbon dioxide
items.misconception: Calcium, carbon and oxygen gas
items.why: Learn the pattern for carbonates such as calcium carbonate: metal carbonate → metal oxide + carbon dioxide.
items.specStatementText: combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions
items.random_wrong: Water and carbon dioxide gas

items.q: Copper is heated in a hot, blue Bunsen flame. Its surface turns black. What is the black layer?
items.correct: Copper oxide, as oxygen joined the copper
items.misconception: Copper changed by heat, with nothing added
items.why: Ask where new material could come from. Air contains oxygen; when a metal is heated in air, oxygen joins on and forms an oxide.
items.specStatementText: combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions
items.random_wrong: Soot (carbon) left on it by the flame

items.q: An iron nail rusts in damp air. None of the rust flakes off. What happens to the mass of the nail and its rust?
items.correct: It goes up, as oxygen from the air joins on
items.misconception: It goes down, as rust eats away the iron
items.why: Rust is a new substance made from iron, oxygen and water. Weigh everything, including the rust: the mass goes up.
items.specStatementText: combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions
items.random_wrong: It stays the same, as rust was already there

items.q: Iron is more reactive than copper. An iron nail is left in blue copper sulfate solution. A brown coating forms. What is it?
items.correct: Copper, pushed out of the copper sulfate
items.misconception: Rust, because the iron nail is wet
items.why: Use the reactivity rule: a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from its compound. The pink-brown metal formed is copper.
items.specStatementText: combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions
items.random_wrong: Iron that has changed into copper

items.q: Which statement is true of every acid?
items.correct: It can be neutralised by an alkali
items.misconception: It eats away any material it touches
items.why: Describe acids by what they react with: an acid is neutralised by an alkali, and it reacts with many metals to make a salt and hydrogen. The metal's atoms end up in the salt.
items.specStatementText: defining acids and alkalis in terms of neutralisation reactions
items.random_wrong: It has the same pH as all other acids

items.q: A substance dissolves in water. Which result shows that the substance is an alkali?
items.correct: It neutralises acids
items.misconception: It turns blue litmus red
items.why: Remember 'red for acid': acids turn blue litmus red.
items.specStatementText: defining acids and alkalis in terms of neutralisation reactions
items.random_wrong: It has a pH below 7

items.q: When an alkali neutralises an acid, what happens to the acid?
items.correct: It reacts with the alkali to make a salt
items.misconception: It breaks down on its own and stops being acid
items.why: Write it as a reaction with two reactants: acid + alkali → salt + water.
items.specStatementText: defining acids and alkalis in terms of neutralisation reactions
items.random_wrong: It is simply stopped from burning anything

items.q: Which statement about the pH scale is correct?
items.correct: Lower numbers are more acidic
items.misconception: Higher numbers are more acidic
items.why: Remember: pH 1 is very acidic, pH 7 is neutral, pH 14 is very alkaline. Going up the scale means less acidic and more alkaline.
items.specStatementText: the pH scale for measuring acidity/alkalinity; and indicators
items.random_wrong: Neutral solutions have a pH of 0

items.q: Universal indicator is green at pH 7, blue at pH 9 and purple at pH 13. A cleaner turns it blue. What does this show?
items.correct: It is less alkaline than a purple liquid
items.misconception: It is as alkaline as a purple liquid
items.why: Read the number: the further below 7, the more acidic; the further above 7, the more alkaline.
items.specStatementText: the pH scale for measuring acidity/alkalinity; and indicators
items.random_wrong: It is more alkaline than purple liquids

items.q: Blue litmus paper is dipped into a solution and stays blue. What does this show?
items.correct: It is not acidic, as an acid turns it red
items.misconception: It is alkaline, as blue means alkali
items.why: Ask what changed. A paper that keeps its starting colour only tells you what the liquid is not; use red litmus or universal indicator to find out more.
items.specStatementText: the pH scale for measuring acidity/alkalinity; and indicators
items.random_wrong: It is acidic, as acids turn litmus blue

items.q: Zinc reacts with hydrochloric acid. One product is zinc chloride. What is the other product?
items.correct: Hydrogen gas, which fizzes off
items.misconception: Water, which stays in the beaker
items.why: Learn them as a pair: a metal gives hydrogen (squeaky pop); an alkali gives water.
items.specStatementText: reactions of acids with metals to produce a salt plus hydrogen
items.random_wrong: Oxygen gas, which fizzes off

items.q: Magnesium reacts with sulfuric acid. Which salt is made?
items.correct: Magnesium sulfate
items.misconception: Sodium chloride
items.why: Name the salt from the reactants: the first part comes from the metal, the second from the acid.
items.specStatementText: reactions of acids with metals to produce a salt plus hydrogen
items.random_wrong: Magnesium acid

items.q: Magnesium is added to hydrochloric acid and it fizzes. Which test shows that the gas is hydrogen?
items.correct: A lit splint gives a squeaky pop
items.misconception: A glowing splint bursts into flame
items.why: Use the word equation: metal + acid → salt + hydrogen. Then use the hydrogen test.
items.specStatementText: reactions of acids with metals to produce a salt plus hydrogen
items.random_wrong: It turns clear limewater milky

items.q: Magnesium ribbon is added to hydrochloric acid. It fizzes and slowly disappears. Where has the magnesium gone?
items.correct: It is now in magnesium chloride, in solution
items.misconception: It is still magnesium, just mixed into the acid
items.why: Ask whether a new substance forms. In a reaction the atoms are rearranged into new molecules; in a mixture the original particles are still there, unchanged.
items.specStatementText: reactions of acids with metals to produce a salt plus hydrogen
items.random_wrong: It has been eaten away to nothing by the acid

items.q: Hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide solution, an alkali. What are the products?
items.correct: Sodium chloride and water
items.misconception: Only the acid, now diluted
items.why: Diluting is not neutralising. Water spreads the acid out; an alkali reacts with it.
items.specStatementText: reactions of acids with alkalis to produce a salt plus water
items.random_wrong: Sodium chloride and hydrogen

items.q: The graph shows the pH as an alkali is slowly added to an acid. Which statement is correct when 20 cm³ of alkali has been added?
items.correct: Some of the acid has been neutralised
items.misconception: No acid has reacted, as the pH is not 7
items.why: Neutralisation is the reaction, not the end point. Some acid is neutralised as soon as any alkali is added.
items.specStatementText: reactions of acids with alkalis to produce a salt plus water
items.random_wrong: It is more acidic than it was at the start

figure.alt: A line graph. The horizontal axis is labelled volume of alkali added (cm³), with marks at 0, 10, 20 and 30. The vertical axis is labelled pH, with marks at 0, 7 and 14, and a dashed line across at pH 7. The line starts at pH 1 at 0 cm³ and rises slowly to about pH 2 at 20 cm³. Near 25 cm³ it rises very steeply through pH 7, then levels off at about pH 12 by 30 cm³.

items.q: Alkali is added to an acid until the pH is exactly 7. The water is then evaporated. What is left?
items.correct: A salt formed by the reaction
items.misconception: Nothing, as they cancel out
items.why: Follow the atoms. Count them before and after: the same atoms are there, joined in new substances. Things that seem to vanish have usually become gases or dissolved substances.
items.specStatementText: reactions of acids with alkalis to produce a salt plus water
items.random_wrong: The acid and alkali, unchanged

items.q: Which statement about a catalyst is correct?
items.correct: It speeds up a reaction and is not used up
items.misconception: It speeds up a reaction but is used up
items.why: A catalyst is given back unchanged. Filter it off and dry it: its mass is the same as at the start.
items.specStatementText: what catalysts do
items.random_wrong: It makes a reaction give more product

items.q: Manganese(IV) oxide speeds up the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. Afterwards, any solid left is filtered off and dried, with none spilled. How does its mass compare with the start?
items.correct: It is the same as at the start
items.misconception: It is more, as it took in oxygen
items.why: Weigh the catalyst before and after: the same mass is recovered, so none of it became product.
items.specStatementText: what catalysts do
items.random_wrong: It is less, as some was used up

items.q: The graph shows the volume of gas made by the same reaction with and without a catalyst. What did the catalyst change?
items.correct: Only how fast the gas was made
items.misconception: The total volume of gas made
items.why: Compare the end points: with or without a catalyst, the same amounts of reactants give the same amount of product.
items.specStatementText: what catalysts do
items.random_wrong: Which gas the reaction made

figure.alt: A line graph. The horizontal axis is labelled time (s), with marks at 0, 100 and 200. The vertical axis is labelled volume of gas (cm³), with marks at 0, 25 and 50. A solid line labelled with catalyst rises steeply and levels off at 50 cm³ after about 60 s. A dashed line labelled without catalyst rises more slowly and levels off at the same height, 50 cm³, after about 150 s.

items.q: Does a colour change always show that a new substance has formed?
items.correct: No. The colour can also change when coloured substances are simply mixed, as when blue and yellow paint make green. You must ask whether a new substance has formed.
items.misconception: A change of colour always means a chemical reaction has happened.
items.why: Signs such as a colour change, fizzing or warming are clues, not proof. Mixing paints changes the colour you see, but the paint particles are unchanged.
items.specStatementText: chemical reactions as the rearrangement of atoms
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: When water boils, do its molecules split into hydrogen and oxygen?
items.correct: No. The water molecules stay whole; they just move far apart as steam. The bubbles in boiling water are water vapour.
items.misconception: Boiling or heating water splits its molecules into hydrogen and oxygen, so the bubbles are hydrogen and oxygen gas.
items.why: Boiling is a change of state. The bubbles are water vapour: the same water molecules, far apart. Splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen needs a chemical reaction.
items.specStatementText: chemical reactions as the rearrangement of atoms
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: In 2H₂O, does the big 2 apply only to the hydrogen?
items.correct: No. The big number applies to the whole formula after it: 2H₂O is two whole water molecules, with 4 hydrogen and 2 oxygen atoms.
items.misconception: A big number in front of a formula multiplies only the first symbol, so 2H₂O is counted as 4 hydrogen atoms but only 1 oxygen atom.
items.why: Read 2H₂O as two lots of H₂O: every atom in the formula is doubled.
items.specStatementText: representing chemical reactions using formulae and using equations
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Does a symbol with no small number after it count as no atoms?
items.correct: No. A symbol with no small number stands for one atom: the 1 is simply not written.
items.misconception: A symbol with no small number after it is not counted, so the O in H₂O counts as no oxygen atoms.
items.why: Every symbol counts. No small number means one atom of that element.
items.specStatementText: representing chemical reactions using formulae and using equations
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Is a symbol equation finished once the formulae are written, or once one element balances?
items.correct: No. A symbol equation is balanced only when every element has the same number of atoms on both sides, so check each element after every change.
items.misconception: A symbol equation is finished once the formulae are written, or once one element balances; the other atoms need not be checked.
items.why: After every change, recount every element on both sides. Stop only when all of them match.
items.specStatementText: representing chemical reactions using formulae and using equations
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Is hydrogen gas written as H, and oxygen gas as O?
items.correct: No. Hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and chlorine gases are made of molecules of two joined atoms, so their formulae are H₂, O₂, N₂ and Cl₂.
items.misconception: The formula of a gaseous element is just its symbol: hydrogen gas is H, oxygen gas is O.
items.why: Learn the elements that exist as pairs of atoms: H₂, O₂, N₂, Cl₂. In equations, always write them with the small 2.
items.specStatementText: representing chemical reactions using formulae and using equations

items.q: When balancing, can a spare atom be written as a product on its own?
items.correct: No. A single oxygen atom is not one of the products. Balance with big numbers so that every atom ends up in a real product: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.
items.misconception: When balancing, a spare atom left over can be written as an extra product on its own (for example Mg + O₂ → MgO + O).
items.why: Only write substances that the reaction really makes. Balance with big numbers in front of the formulae you were given.
items.specStatementText: representing chemical reactions using formulae and using equations

items.q: In a word equation, does it matter which side the products go on?
items.correct: Yes. The reactants (what you start with) go on the left of the arrow, and the products (what is made) go on the right.
items.misconception: The reactants and products can be written on either side of the arrow, so a product may go on the left.
items.why: The arrow points from what you start with to what is made. Read it as 'reacts to make'.
items.specStatementText: representing chemical reactions using formulae and using equations

items.q: Does the arrow in a word equation mean 'equals'?
items.correct: No. The arrow means 'reacts to make'. The products are new substances, not the same as the reactants.
items.misconception: The arrow in an equation means 'equals', so an equals sign can be used instead.
items.why: Write an arrow from reactants to products. It shows a change, not that the two sides are the same substances.

items.q: When a fuel burns, does it turn into energy?
items.correct: No. The atoms of the fuel end up in new substances (carbon dioxide and water). Energy is transferred as heat and light, but no matter turns into energy.
items.misconception: When a fuel burns, the fuel (or part of it) turns into heat and light energy.
items.why: Follow the atoms: they go into the gases made. The energy is transferred by the reaction; atoms do not turn into energy.

items.q: Does everything that burns or is heated strongly make carbon dioxide and water?
items.correct: No. Carbon dioxide and water come from fuels that contain carbon and hydrogen. A metal burns to its oxide, and a heated metal carbonate gives a metal oxide and carbon dioxide.
items.misconception: Anything that burns or is heated strongly makes carbon dioxide and water, as fuels do.
items.why: Use the atoms you start with. Products can only contain elements that were in the reactants.
items.specStatementText: combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: When a substance is heated strongly, does it only melt or evaporate?
items.correct: Not always. Burning and thermal decomposition make new substances. A candle's wax does melt and evaporate, but the wax vapour then reacts with oxygen in the flame.
items.misconception: When a substance is heated strongly or burns, it only melts or evaporates; no new substance forms.
items.why: Look for a new substance: a gas that was not there before, or a solid with different properties. If one forms, it is a reaction, not just a change of state.
items.specStatementText: combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions

items.q: Was the rust already in the nail before it rusted?
items.correct: No. Rust is a new substance that forms when iron reacts with oxygen and water from the air.
items.misconception: The rust was already there inside or under the surface of the nail and just comes out, so the mass stays the same.
items.why: Rust needs oxygen and water from outside the nail: a nail kept in dry air does not rust.
items.specStatementText: combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions

items.q: Do gases such as air and oxygen have mass?
items.correct: Yes. Gases are made of particles, and every particle has mass. When a gas joins a solid the mass goes up; when a gas escapes the mass goes down.
items.misconception: Gases, including air and oxygen, have no mass, so a gas joining on or leaving cannot change the mass.
items.why: A sealed flask of air is heavier than the same flask with the air pumped out. Every gas has mass.
items.specStatementText: combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions

items.q: Does an acid bubble and fizz on its own?
items.correct: No. An acid on its own does not fizz. Bubbles appear when it reacts with something: with a metal, the bubbles are hydrogen.
items.misconception: Acids bubble and fizz by themselves, so the bubbles seen in an acid are the acid itself.
items.why: Bubbles mean a gas is being made by a reaction. Ask what is reacting with the acid, then test the gas.

items.q: Are alkalis harmless substances that only stop acids from working?
items.correct: No. Alkalis such as sodium hydroxide solution can damage skin and eyes just as acids can, and they react with other substances too. An alkali reacts with an acid; it does not just block it.
items.misconception: Alkalis are harmless and do nothing on their own; they only stop acids from burning or eating things.
items.why: Treat alkalis with the same care as acids. In neutralisation the alkali and the acid both react to make new substances.
items.specStatementText: defining acids and alkalis in terms of neutralisation reactions

items.q: Is a neutral liquid at pH 0?
items.correct: No. Neutral is pH 7, in the middle of the scale. pH 0 is extremely acidic.
items.misconception: Neutral is pH 0, so any pH above 0 is alkaline.
items.why: Picture the scale with 7 in the middle: acids below 7, alkalis above.
items.specStatementText: the pH scale for measuring acidity/alkalinity; and indicators
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: If an indicator does not change colour, must the liquid be neutral?
items.correct: No. Blue litmus does not change in an alkali either. A neutral liquid has pH 7, which universal indicator shows as green.
items.misconception: If an indicator paper does not change colour, the liquid must be neutral.
items.why: Use universal indicator (green at pH 7), or test with both red and blue litmus: a neutral liquid changes neither.

items.q: Does a metal reacting with an acid make the metal oxide?
items.correct: No. A metal reacting with an acid makes a salt and hydrogen. With hydrochloric acid the salt is a chloride, such as zinc chloride.
items.misconception: When a metal reacts with an acid it makes the metal oxide.
items.why: Check the reactants: no oxygen gas is used. The metal takes the place of the hydrogen in the acid, making a salt.
items.specStatementText: reactions of acids with metals to produce a salt plus hydrogen

items.q: Is every salt a chloride?
items.correct: No. The salt's name comes from the acid: hydrochloric acid makes chlorides, sulfuric acid makes sulfates, nitric acid makes nitrates.
items.misconception: Every salt is a chloride, whichever acid is used.
items.why: Match the acid to the ending: hydrochloric → chloride, sulfuric → sulfate, nitric → nitrate.
items.specStatementText: reactions of acids with metals to produce a salt plus hydrogen
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Is the fizzing gas from a metal in an acid carbon dioxide?
items.correct: No. A metal and an acid make hydrogen. Carbon dioxide can only form if carbon is present, and there is no carbon in magnesium or hydrochloric acid.
items.misconception: Any fizzing gas is carbon dioxide, so a metal fizzing in an acid gives off carbon dioxide.
items.why: Check the atoms: no carbon, no carbon dioxide. Test the gas: a squeaky pop shows hydrogen.
items.specStatementText: reactions of acids with metals to produce a salt plus hydrogen
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Does the name of a salt keep the word 'acid'?
items.correct: No. A salt is not an acid. Its name has two parts: the metal, then chloride, sulfate or nitrate (for example magnesium sulfate, sodium chloride).
items.misconception: The salt's name keeps the word acid, as in 'magnesium acid' or 'sodium chloride acid'.
items.why: Drop the word acid, because the acid has reacted. Use the ending chloride, sulfate or nitrate.

items.q: Does a catalyst change which products a reaction makes?
items.correct: No. A catalyst speeds up the same reaction, so the same products form.
items.misconception: A catalyst changes which products are made, as if it were another reactant.
items.why: The reaction is the same with or without the catalyst; only its speed changes.
items.specStatementText: what catalysts do
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Can a reaction happen at all without its catalyst?
items.correct: Yes. The same reaction still happens without the catalyst, but more slowly.
items.misconception: A reaction cannot happen at all without its catalyst; the catalyst is what makes it happen.
items.why: A catalyst changes how fast a reaction goes, not whether it goes.
items.specStatementText: what catalysts do
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid and gives off a gas. Is the gas acidic?
items.correct: No. The gas is hydrogen, which is not acidic. It is a new substance made in the reaction, not the acid itself.
items.misconception: The gas given off when a metal reacts with an acid is acidic, because it comes from the acid.
items.why: The gas is hydrogen, a new substance made in the reaction. Test it with a lit splint: hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop.
